body:
Water supply and wastewater disposal

Water management involves obtaining water, making it available for use, storing it where necessary and removing used water. Harappan cities developed different arrangements to meet these needs.

It is important to distinguish water supply from drainage. Wells and reservoirs supplied or stored water. Drains carried away wastewater or, in some locations, directed stormwater towards storage facilities.

Wells at Mohenjodaro

Mohenjodaro is especially notable for its numerous brick-lined wells. Wells provided access to groundwater and were distributed through residential areas.

Some wells were situated within houses. Others could be approached from spaces accessible to people outside an individual household.

Scholars have estimated that Mohenjodaro contained approximately 700 wells. This is an archaeological estimate rather than an exact count of every well that existed during the city's occupation.

Wells helped households obtain water for bathing, washing and other daily activities. Their close association with residential buildings and bathrooms is a distinctive feature of Mohenjodaro's urban infrastructure.

Reservoirs at Dholavira

Water management took a different form at Dholavira, situated on Khadir Bet in the Rann of Kutch, Gujarat. The surrounding environment had limited dependable freshwater sources, making water storage especially important.

Dholavira had a sophisticated network of reservoirs and water channels. The city's inhabitants made use of rainfall and seasonal watercourses, directing water towards storage areas.

Several reservoirs were constructed with stone masonry or cut into the natural rock. Some were connected with channels that helped collect or move water.

The NCERT Class 6 account records that Dholavira had at least 6 large reservoirs and that its largest reservoir measured approximately 73 m in length.

These facilities demonstrate how urban planning could respond to local geographical conditions. Where Mohenjodaro relied extensively on wells, Dholavira invested heavily in storing water collected during periods when it was available.

Different water sources required different solutions

FacilityMain functionIllustrative site
Brick-lined wellObtaining groundwaterMohenjodaro
ReservoirStoring collected waterDholavira
Household drainRemoving used domestic waterMohenjodaro
Stormwater channelDirecting collected rainwaterDholavira

These systems had different purposes. A reservoir was not simply a large drain, and a covered wastewater channel was not necessarily a source of drinking water.

Water management and organised construction

Wells, reservoirs and drainage networks required careful construction. Reservoirs also needed suitable channels and maintenance if they were to remain useful.

The scale and coordination visible in these structures indicate that Harappan builders could organise substantial public works. However, the architecture alone does not establish the exact form of government or the identity of the people who directed construction.

Mohenjodaro: Numerous wells and connected household drainage.

Dholavira: Large reservoirs, channels and water harvesting suited to a relatively dry environment.

Prelims focus

  • Mohenjodaro is famous for its numerous brick-lined wells.
  • Approximately 700 wells have been estimated for Mohenjodaro.
  • Dholavira is particularly associated with reservoirs and water harvesting.
  • Dholavira's largest recorded reservoir was approximately 73 m long in the cited NCERT account.
  • Wells, storage reservoirs and wastewater drains perform different functions.
  • Trap: Do not confuse Dholavira's water-storage reservoirs with Mohenjodaro's Great Bath.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Chapter 1, Section 3.2, Domestic architecture, p. 7; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 6, Water Management, pp. 94–95; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Dholavira: a Harappan City, Brief Synthesis and Criterion (iv), consulted 17 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Mohenjodaro wells obtain groundwater and drains remove wastewater; Dholavira channels collect seasonal water into reservoirs for storage.
pictures.caption: Different functions of wells, reservoirs and drainage channels.

title: Wells, Reservoirs and Water Management in Harappan Cities

body:
Public architecture in Harappan cities

Besides residential houses, Harappan settlements contained large or distinctive structures that probably served collective, administrative, storage-related or ceremonial purposes.

Some of these buildings are identified with reasonable confidence by their physical features. Others are traditionally called granaries, assembly halls or warehouses, although their exact functions remain uncertain.

The most important example of a clearly identifiable water-related public structure is the Great Bath at Mohenjodaro.

The Great Bath at Mohenjodaro

The Great Bath was constructed within the Citadel of Mohenjodaro. It consisted of a large rectangular brick-lined tank within a courtyard, with a corridor surrounding the tank.

The tank measured approximately 12 m in length and 7 m in width. Flights of steps led down into it from the northern and southern ends.

The structure included several important architectural features:

  • Rectangular bathing tank: A substantial basin constructed with carefully arranged bricks.
  • Steps: Flights of steps at the northern and southern ends provided access to the water.
  • Waterproofing: Bricks were carefully laid and gypsum mortar was used to reduce water leakage. Natural bitumen, a tar-like substance, was also used as waterproofing material.
  • Surrounding spaces: The tank was enclosed by corridors and associated rooms.
  • Water supply: A large well was located in an adjoining room and was probably connected with the provision of water.
  • Water outlet: A substantial drain allowed water to be discharged from the tank.

What was the Great Bath used for?

The Great Bath was evidently designed for activities involving water, but its exact social or religious function is not established.

Its distinctive construction and location within the Citadel have led to the suggestion that it was used for special ceremonial or ritual bathing.

This interpretation is plausible, but it should not be treated as a demonstrated fact. The Great Bath cannot be confidently described as a swimming pool, a royal bathing room or a temple merely from its architecture.

The existence and physical design of the Great Bath are well established. Its precise purpose remains uncertain. A possible ritual function is an interpretation, not a confirmed historical fact.

Large buildings called granaries

Some large Harappan buildings have traditionally been described as granaries. A granary is a building used to store harvested grain.

The best-known example is the large structure at Harappa's Mound F. Its surviving foundations consist of substantial brickwork arranged into 2 parallel rows of 6 rectangular units, separated by a central passage. These structural remains have long been interpreted as parts of a large storage building.

However, the identification as a granary is disputed. Excavations have not provided sufficiently clear evidence, such as concentrations of stored grain, to establish that this large structure was actually used for grain storage.

It is therefore more precise to call it the so-called Granary at Harappa or the large building traditionally identified as a granary.

Large structures at Mohenjodaro

Mohenjodaro also had a massive building on the Citadel that has been described as a granary or warehouse. Its substantial brick foundations survive, while parts of the upper structure, possibly constructed from wood, have disappeared.

Like the structure at Harappa, its exact function remains uncertain.

Other large buildings at Mohenjodaro have been called an Assembly Hall or a Pillared Hall. Their scale and arrangement suggest special uses, but their original functions cannot be established merely from these names.

Storehouses and ceremonial installations

Lothal in Gujarat contained a structure identified as a warehouse or storehouse. Seals and clay seal impressions recovered from this area provide evidence consistent with the handling and storage of goods.

At Kalibangan and Lothal, certain structural installations have been interpreted as fire altars. These may have been associated with ceremonial activities, although their precise use is not fully established.

What public buildings reveal

Large platforms, storage-related structures, bathing facilities and distinctive installations demonstrate that Harappan towns contained buildings serving purposes beyond individual household residence.

Nevertheless, no structure can be conclusively identified as a royal palace or temple simply because it is large, elevated or architecturally unusual.

Prelims focus

  • The Great Bath was located in the Citadel of Mohenjodaro.
  • Its tank measured approximately 12 m × 7 m.
  • Steps descended into the Great Bath from the north and south.
  • Gypsum mortar and natural bitumen were used in its waterproof construction.
  • Harappa's Mound F contains the large structure traditionally called a granary.
  • Kalibangan and Lothal have installations interpreted as fire altars.
  • Trap: The identification of a large Harappan building as a granary does not prove that grain was stored there.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6 History, Chapter 4, In the Earliest Cities, p. 33; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Chapter 1, Section 3.3, The Citadel, p. 8; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 6, pp. 91–93; Jonathan Mark Kenoyer, Granary, Harappa, Around the Indus in 90 Slides, Harappa.com, consulted 17 November 2026; Harappa Archaeological Research Project, Granary Area, Harappa.com, consulted 17 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The principal architectural features of the Great Bath at Mohenjodaro.

title: The Great Bath, Granaries and Other Public Buildings

body:
Location and importance

Dholavira is an important Harappan archaeological site situated on Khadir Bet in the Rann of Kutch, Gujarat.

It provides one of the clearest examples of how Harappan urban planning could be adapted to local geographical conditions. Its distinctive features include a complex division of the settlement, extensive fortifications, substantial stone construction and a sophisticated system of water storage.

Dholavira was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2021, in recognition of its outstanding archaeological and urban significance.

The 3 principal urban divisions

Unlike the common Harappan pattern of a Citadel and Lower Town, Dholavira is generally described as having 3 major urban divisions:

  1. Citadel or central fortified complex: The elevated, strongly defended section, including the area described as the Castle and its associated Bailey.
  2. Middle Town: A separately organised residential section with planned streets and substantial buildings.
  3. Lower Town: Another residential section within the wider settlement, containing houses and streets.

The city also contained a substantial ceremonial ground and other open spaces associated with its fortified central complex.

The terms Castle and Bailey describe archaeological sections of the site. They should not be taken as proof that Dholavira possessed a monarchy identical to later historical kingdoms.

Fortifications and gateways

Dholavira had extensive fortification walls surrounding and separating important urban areas. The Castle was especially heavily fortified, and the Middle Town also had a distinctive fortified enclosure.

Gateways provided controlled entrances between different parts of the city. The surviving structures indicate substantial investment in organising the settlement and constructing its boundaries.

Stone masonry was particularly prominent at Dholavira. Builders made extensive use of locally available stone, often in combination with mud-brick construction.

This is a significant distinction from Mohenjodaro, where baked-brick structures are especially prominent.

Water harvesting and reservoirs

Dholavira was located in a relatively dry environment where obtaining and preserving water was essential.

The settlement made use of 2 seasonal streams and channels that helped collect or direct water. Substantial reservoirs were constructed around the fortified core, particularly towards its eastern and southern sides.

Some reservoirs were built with stone masonry, while others were partly cut into natural rock. This required substantial construction work but allowed water to be stored for later use.

At least 6 large reservoirs are described in the NCERT Class 6 account, with the largest recorded there as approximately 73 m long.

Buildings and public spaces

The settlement contained houses of different sizes, streets, gateways and open areas. Its planned arrangement suggests that different parts of the city served different purposes.

A large open area associated with the central complex is commonly described as a ceremonial ground. It may have accommodated gatherings or collective activities, although specific events held there cannot be established with certainty.

Large signs of the Harappan script were also found at Dholavira, associated with an entrance area. These are notable because many other Harappan inscriptions occur on much smaller objects, especially seals.

Why Dholavira is an important comparison

Dholavira shows that Harappan urban planning did not depend on a single type of building material or a single method of obtaining water.

It combined a distinctively organised and fortified settlement with extensive stone architecture and water-harvesting facilities suited to the conditions of Kutch.

Dholavira in one connection

Its distinctive identity lies in the combination of a 3-part town arrangement, extensive stone fortifications and large water-storage reservoirs.

Prelims focus

  • Dholavira is situated on Khadir Bet in the Rann of Kutch, Gujarat.
  • It is generally described as having 3 principal urban divisions.
  • Its central complex included the Castle and Bailey.
  • Dholavira is particularly associated with stone construction, fortifications and reservoirs.
  • Seasonal watercourses contributed to its water-harvesting arrangements.
  • Dholavira was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2021.
  • Trap: Dholavira should not be described as having only the conventional Citadel–Lower Town arrangement.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6 History, Chapter 4, In the Earliest Cities, p. 39; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 6, pp. 91–95; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 2, Arts of the Indus Valley, p. 15; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Dholavira: a Harappan City, Brief Synthesis, Outstanding Universal Value and World Heritage List entry, consulted 17 November 2026.]
